transcript:
Header
Date: 2025-12-18
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Reed (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Lyra, Head of ML), Tom Redd (Lyra, Platform), Priya Suresh (Lyra, PM)

Summary:
Short scoping session focused on POC success criteria, workload sizing, and building a cost model for Lyra's retrieval-augmented generation workloads. Agreed to run definitive benchmarks (latency/throughput) with provided prompt sets and to iterate on per-token unit economics including batching and caching knobs. Action items and deadlines captured below.

Agenda:
1) Introductions & goals
2) Lyra workload overview (qps, seq lengths, prompt distribution)
3) Success criteria for the POC and timelines
4) Cost modeling approach (per-token vs per-request, batching, caching, quantization)
5) Benchmark plan and next steps

Transcript:
00:00 - Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick ping, can you all hear me?
00:04 - Aisha: Yep good here, thanks, Maya.
00:06 - Tom: loud and clear.
00:08 - Maya: Awesome. So agenda for today, we wanna scope a POC — cost modeling specifically — and figure out what benchmarks you need to feel comfortable. Jonas will jump into some throughput/latency stuff, but first can you share a little bit about the workload?
00:25 - Aisha: Sure. So at Lyra we run a customer support assistant that does retrieval-augmented generation. The core is about short answers, sometimes longer summaries. Distribution is about 70% short (<128 tokens), 25% medium (128-512), 5% long (>512). Peak QPS around 80 at the moment but we expect spikes to 250 for flash events.
00:47 - Priya: And the success criteria from product side is <400ms p50 for short queries, and p95 under 1.2s for short as well. For longer ones we have looser goals but want to know cost tradeoffs.
01:05 - Jonas: Right, and just to be clear, when you say 80 QPS steady, is that concurrent requests or sustained QPS across the fleet?
01:12 - Aisha: Sustained across the fleet. We have a load balancer and a microservice layer that fans out. We can give per-customer buckets if helpful.
01:20 - Maya: That's super helpful. For the cost model we typically break down per-token inference cost, overhead (request/response), and then amortize fixed infra for dedicated options. We also add knobs like batching, KV cache hit rates, and quantization profiles.
01:36 - Tom: quick question — when you say KV cache, do you mean prefix caching or the memory-based K V cache? Sometimes in our notes it was written as K V cash and I wanna make sure.
01:45 - Jonas: yeah it's the KV cache, prefix caching for recently used contexts. On some long-tail prompts we see low hit rates but for sessionized flows it's higher.
01:54 - Aisha: Our average KV hit is like 26% today. We think with small infra changes we can push to ~40%.
02:02 - Maya: Great, that 26% is actually a big lever in the model. If we assume 40% hit rate in the POC we can show meaningful token savings.
02:12 - Priya: On timelines, we ideally want a POC outcome by end of January. A small pilot in mid-January and then a readout. Is that plausible?
02:22 - Jonas: Depends on benchmark scope. If we restrict to hosted API + one dedicated variant and the same model family (we can run fp16 and an int8-ish quantized variant), we can get numbers in 2-3 weeks. If you want on-prem/private or custom compilation that adds time.
02:36 - Aisha: We'll start hosted, then consider dedicated. Private is a hard requirement for a few regulated customers but not for the entire POC.
02:44 - Maya: Sounds fair. For the cost model inputs please share token distribution (you gave a rough breakdown), average request size incl. context, and monthly QPS curve. We will populate a spreadsheet with per-token estimates under different batch and quantization scenarios.
02:59 - Tom: Can you outline what the per-token estimate will include? I.e., raw GPU op cost, infra overhead, data egress?
03:06 - Maya: Yes. Roughly: compute per-token (based on GPU throughput at the observed seq length), networking and I/O overhead, fixed instance amortization (for dedicated), and software/service margin. For hosted we give a blended per-token that includes multi-tenant overhead. We'll show both hosted and dedicated units.
03:20 - Aisha: do you handle function calling / streaming charges differently?
03:24 - Jonas: Streaming is usually charged similarly but we model that some streaming requests result in extra tokens due to chunking. Function calling is modeled as extra tokens for tool responses. We'll ask for a percent of requests that use streaming so we can model that.
03:36 - Priya: Would you recommend starting POC with a smaller model for cost benchmarking then scale to production-size models?
03:41 - Jonas: We typically run a 2-model approach: a mid-sized open model for high-throughput baseline and the production target model to measure quality and worst-case latency. This gives you both cost curves and quality delta.
03:54 - Maya: On batching, we want to capture two knobs: batching window (ms) and max batch size. Increasing batching reduces per-token cost but increases latency for singletons. We'll run sensitivity analysis with your p50/p95 targets.
04:10 - Aisha: For our product we can't accept p50 regressions over 50ms for short queries, otherwise UX suffers.
04:18 - Jonas: Noted. We'll include a chart showing batching vs p50/p95 and cost per 1k tokens.
04:27 - Maya: Ok let's talk benchmarks: we propose a matrix across seq lengths (64, 256, 512), batch sizes (1, 4, 16, 32), and two quantization profiles (fp16 and int8/quantized). We'll measure p50/p95 latencies and throughput until we saturate.
04:45 - Tom: Do you simulate KV cache hits or do you run a warm cache?
04:49 - Jonas: We can do both. Warm cache run for hit rate simulation and synthetic hit rate injection for scenarios where you want 40% or 60% hits.
04:58 - Aisha: And how will you measure real-world CPU overhead on our microservices? We care about CPU bottlenecks on the fan-out layer.
05:05 - Maya: For hosted runs we measure endpoint CPU and network egress. For dedicated we can run a small agent to capture your microservice CPU. But we'd need short-lived access or run synthetic clients that mirror fan-out.
05:18 - Priya: Security questions — we need SOC 2 docs and SSO/SAML integrations. Also curious about audit logs for Private.
05:25 - Maya: We'll send SOC 2 and the security playbook. For Private, audit logs and KMS integrations are supported; we'll include the architecture doc in the follow-up.
05:33 - Aisha: Competitors asked us about unit economics — OpenAI gave a blended cost that was lower in their pitch. How do you handle comparisons?
05:40 - Maya: We try to do apples-to-apples: same prompt set, same response length assumptions, and account for batching/caching differences. Often the difference is in the overhead assumptions and whether they include quiescent infra. We'll show an annotated spreadsheet so you can see where numbers diverge.
05:57 - Tom: On pricing models, can you do both usage-based and reserved capacity simulations? We need to justify both to finance.
06:03 - Jonas: Yep. We'll show per-token for usage-based and effective per-token after amortizing commit levels (monthly/annual) for dedicated pools, including burst capacity options.
06:12 - Priya: For the POC success criteria, we want: 1) Verified p50/p95 under targeted loads for short queries, 2) cost per 1k tokens under X threshold for steady state, and 3) documentation of any integration blockers for Private deployment. Is that aligned?
06:27 - Maya: That's perfect. We'll add a quality gate comparing mid-sized model to production model on answer accuracy for a small eval set you provide.
06:36 - Aisha: We'll provide ~200 labeled prompts for eval. Also want to capture abnormal cases — multi-turn sessions.
06:43 - Jonas: Great. For multi-turn we'll simulate session stickiness to measure KV cache hit benefits.
06:49 - Maya: Let's capture a sample cost example live: assume short query 50 tokens response, avg 75 tokens total including prompt. If hosted per-token compute is $0.000012 per token under current multi-tenant assumptions, that's about $0.009 per 1k tokens for compute only. With network + margin maybe $0.012 per 1k. But numbers will change with batching and quantization.
07:15 - Tom: Wait can you repeat that math? I think you said $0.000012 per token?
07:19 - Maya: Yup, compute-only baseline. So 1k tokens is 1000 * 0.000012 = 0.012, sorry I mis-spoke earlier. So compute only about $0.012 per 1k, add overhead gets to ~$0.015 per 1k in hosted.
07:32 - Aisha: How much does moving to dedicated reduce that?
07:35 - Jonas: If you have consistent usage (they gave numbers earlier) with a commit we usually see effective per-token drop of 30-45% depending on utilization and model. So from $0.015 hosted to maybe $0.008-0.01 for ded.
07:47 - Priya: That delta is big. We'll need both scenarios for Finance.
07:50 - Maya: Totally. We'll model a utilization curve in the spreadsheet.
07:54 - Aisha: Any advice on initial batching window? We worry about latency but want cost benefits.
07:58 - Jonas: Start with a small window like 10-20ms and max batch 8 for short queries, and run experiments. We find diminishing returns after batch 16 for these seq lengths.
08:09 - Tom: For quantization, do you have recommended profiles for our model family?
08:13 - Jonas: For transformer-based open models, int8 quantization usually reduces throughput slightly but cuts memory and allows more concurrency; check quality regression but we have real-world profiles that often preserve quality. We'll include quality vs quantization table.
08:26 - Aisha: Regarding instrumentation, what telemetry will Redwood need from us?
08:30 - Maya: For the benchmark we only need sample clients and tokenized prompt sets. For production sizing, optionally logs for token distribution and request latencies. We'll provide a lightweight harness for load tests.
08:41 - Priya: Let's talk about legal/procurement — if we go to dedicated, how long is typical lead time?
08:47 - Maya: For Dedicated it's usually a 30-60 day lead time depending on region and capacity. Private deployments can be longer (60-90 days) and need more security review.
08:57 - Aisha: Ok, that aligns with our Jan/Feb timeline.
09:01 - Jonas: For benchmarking we'll propose two phases: Phase 1 hosted baseline (1 week), Phase 2 dedicated variant + quantized runs (1-2 weeks). Phase 1 feeds into cost model and Phase 2 confirms production assumptions.
09:15 - Tom: One last question — do you include developer/ops overhead in cost per token? We want total cost of ownership.
09:21 - Maya: We can include a discretionary line for DevOps/monitoring and SLA-costs. Typically we add an ops multiplier (2-5%) or a fixed monthly cost depending on your internal model.
09:33 - Priya: Great. Any risks we should note?
09:36 - Jonas: Latency tail sensitivity to batch mixing, quantization quality regressions on certain prompts, and KV cache hit variability. We'll surface these in risk register in the follow-up.
09:47 - Aisha: Perfect. I'm comfortable with the plan. Let's talk logistics for the benchmark — we prefer the live run on 12/30 or 12/31 to avoid holidays, but week of 12/29 also works.
09:58 - Maya: We'll propose a couple of slots in the follow-up.
10:02 - Maya: Alright let's recap action items and owners.
10:05 - Maya: Action item 1: Maya send cost model spreadsheet and ask for prompt sets and QPS curves (due 12/20). Action item 2: Jonas draft benchmark matrix (due 12/22). Action item 3: Lyra to provide eval prompts and token distributions (due 12/23).
10:22 - Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
10:24 - Tom: Thanks.
10:25 - Aisha: Thanks, talk soon.

Auto-summary (optional):
- POC goals: Verify latency SLOs for short queries, validate cost per 1k tokens under different deployment models, and identify integration blockers for Private deployment.
- Benchmark plan: matrix across seq lengths, batch sizes, and quantization; warm and synthetic cache-hit runs; measure p50/p95 and throughput.
- Cost model to include per-token compute, infra amortization for dedicated, networking and ops overhead, and sensitivity to batching/kv-cache/quantization.
